questions.knowledge_point: Listing the Elements of a Set Defined Over a Finite or Infinite Set
questions.problem:
Consider the set $A,$ defined as

$$
A={\frac{2n}{n+1}:n\in {1,2,3,4}}.
$$

Which of the following sets is equivalent to $A?$
questions.worked_solution:
The elements of $A$ are all the terms of the sequence ${a}_{n},$ given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2n}{n+1},\,n\in {1,2,3,4}.
$$

Let's write down all the terms of our sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =\frac{2(1)}{1+1}=1 \\ {a}_{2} & =\frac{2(2)}{2+1}=\frac{4}{3} \\ {a}_{3} & =\frac{2(3)}{3+1}=\frac{3}{2} \\ {a}_{4} & =\frac{2(4)}{4+1}=\frac{8}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
A={1,\frac{4}{3},\frac{3}{2},\frac{8}{5}}.
$$

provenance.kp_title: Listing the Elements of a Set Defined Over a Finite or Infinite Set

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Complement of a Set Given Using Ellipsis Notation
questions.problem: Let $U={a,b,c,…,z}$ be the universal set and $Y={a,b,c,…,w}$, then $\overset{―}{Y}=$
questions.worked_solution:
The complement of $Y,$ denoted $\overset{―}{Y},$ consists of every element in the universal set $U$ that is not in the set $Y.$

The universal set $U$ consists of the letters $a$ through $z,$ while the set $Y$ consists of the letters $a$ through $w.$

So, the only elements of $U$ that are not in $Y$ are the letters $x$ through $z.$

Therefore, the complement of $Y$ is

$$
\overset{―}{Y}={x,y,z}.
$$

provenance.kp_title: Finding the Complement of a Set Given Using Ellipsis Notation

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating an Integral Given Another Integral With Reversed Limits of Integration
questions.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-6}^{-1}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{-1}^{-6}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=-9\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can split up the given integral using the sum rule and factor out the constants. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-6}^{-1}(3f(x)+8)\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{-6}^{-1}f(x)\,\text{d}x\,+\,8{\int }_{-6}^{-1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3(-9)\,+\,8\cdot x\,{|}_{-6}^{-1} \\  & =-27\,+\,8((-1)-(-6)) \\  & =-27\,+\,40 \\  & =13.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Evaluating an Integral Given Another Integral With Reversed Limits of Integration

questions.knowledge_point: Dividing an Imaginary Number by a Complex Number
questions.worked_solution:
The denominator is $-5+4\text{i}$ and its conjugate is $-5-4\text{i}.$ We multiply both the numerator and the denominator by $-5-4\text{i},$ so that the denominator turns into a real number:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{9\text{i}}{-5+4\text{i}} & =\frac{9\text{i}}{-5+4\text{i}}\cdot \frac{-5-4\text{i}}{-5-4\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{-45\text{i}-36{\text{i}}^{2}}{{5}^{2}-{4}^{2}{\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-45\text{i}-36(-1)}{{5}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{36-45\text{i}}{25+16} \\  & =\frac{36-45\text{i}}{41}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the denominator is a real number, we can write the complex number in the form $a+b\text{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{36-45\text{i}}{41}=\frac{36}{41}-\frac{45}{41}\text{i}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Dividing an Imaginary Number by a Complex Number

questions.worked_solution:
Let $u={log}_{5}⁡({x}^{3}).$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\,⟹\,\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}{3}\text{d}u=\frac{\text{d}x}{x}.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{log}_{5}⁡({x}^{3})}{2x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int {log}_{5}⁡({x}^{3})\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{x} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int u\cdot (\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}{3}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}{6}\int u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}{6}\cdot \frac{{u}^{2}}{2}+C \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡5{log}_{5}^{2}⁡({x}^{3})}{12}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Area Bounded Above a Curve and Below the X-Axis
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14101012/assets/b98d1dd70f315b3059f639c749e83e4679ee9f1fe23682285b789a6e03ee0978.png)

Find the area between the curve $y=-5{x}^{2}+2x-1$, the $x$-axis and the lines $x=0$ and $x=1$, shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the area, we just need to compute the corresponding definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-5{x}^{2}+2x-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-5{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x+2{\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x-1{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-5\cdot {\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{1}+2\cdot {\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}|}_{0}^{1}-1\cdot x{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-5(\frac{1}{3}-0)+2(\frac{1}{2}-0)-1(1-0) \\  & =-\frac{5}{3}+1-1 \\  & =-\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we obtained a negative number. So the area that we want is $\frac{5}{3}.$

provenance.kp_title: Calculating the Area Bounded Above a Curve and Below the X-Axis

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Area of the Parallelogram Spanned by Two Parallel Vectors
questions.worked_solution:
First, we construct a matrix where the columns are made up of the components of the corresponding vectors:

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & a\end{aligned}]
$$

Then, we find the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(M) & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & a\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot a-1\cdot 4 \\  & =2a-4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, setting the expression for the determinant equal to $0$ and solving for $a,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2a-4 & =0 \\ 2a & =4 \\ a & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Calculating the Area of the Parallelogram Spanned by Two Parallel Vectors

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Angle Between Two Vectors Given Their Components
questions.problem: Find the angle between $a=⟨3,1,1⟩$ and $b=⟨1,3,1⟩.$ Round your answer to the nearest degree.
questions.worked_solution:
Rearranging the dot product formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,a\,||\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{x}{b}_{x}+{a}_{y}{b}_{y}+{a}_{z}{b}_{z}}{\sqrt{{a}_{x}^{2}+{a}_{y}^{2}+{a}_{z}^{2}}\sqrt{{b}_{x}^{2}+{b}_{y}^{2}+{b}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{3\cdot 1+1\cdot 3+1\cdot 1}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{7}{\sqrt{11}\cdot \sqrt{11}} \\  & =\frac{7}{11}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{7}{11})≈{50}^{∘}.
$$

provenance.kp_title: Finding the Angle Between Two Vectors Given Their Components

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Degree of a Product of Polynomials
questions.problem: If $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ are polynomials of degree $4$ and $9$, respectively,  the degree of $P\cdot Q$ is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Since $P$ is a polynomial of degree $4,$ the leading term contains an ${x}^{4}.$

Since $Q$ is a polynomial of degree $9,$ the leading term contains an ${x}^{9}.$

In $P\cdot Q,$ the ${x}^{4}$ term in $P$ multiplies with the ${x}^{9}$ term in $Q$ to form a term containing ${x}^{4}\cdot {x}^{9}={x}^{4+9}={x}^{13}.$

Therefore, the degree of $P\cdot Q$ must be $13.$

provenance.kp_title: Identifying the Degree of a Product of Polynomials

questions.knowledge_point: Sets Defined Using Quadratic Equations and Inequalities
questions.worked_solution:
The elements of the given set are the positive real numbers that satisfy the inequality ${x}^{2}-1\le 15.$ 

So, we first need to solve our inequality for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-1 & \le 15 \\ {x}^{2} & \le 16 \\ \sqrt{{x}^{2}} & \le \sqrt{16} \\ |x| & \le 4 \\ -4\le x & \le 4\end{aligned}
$$

The positive real numbers that are solutions to the inequality above are $x\in (0,4].$ Therefore, the given set can be written as 

$$
A=(0,4].
$$

provenance.kp_title: Sets Defined Using Quadratic Equations and Inequalities
